set.statement: In two US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had met, or were estimated to meet at some time in their life, criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey and 31.9% for tobacco (tobacco dependence was assessed, for daily smoking only, in a subsample of 4,414 and divided by tobacco use taken from another 1991 national survey, so it has no standard error); among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, and half of the people who became dependent had done so within about 5 years of first use; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. Two of these reviews also give about 1 in 10 for other groups without data of their own: Connor et al. (2021), citing a UN report, for people who use cannabis worldwide and for people who use it regularly, and Hall (2015), in its abstract, for people who use it regularly. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). Higher figures from more recent US national data use other definitions and denominators: Connor et al. (2021) cite about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and a 2020 professional statement gives 3 in 10 people who had used cannabis in the past year as meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis of the 2012 to 2013 survey; second-hand); the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In two large US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis, even once, had been dependent on it or were expected to become dependent at some point in their life, using an older, narrower definition of dependence. In the 1990 to 1992 survey this was fewer than for tobacco (about 32 in 100), heroin (23), cocaine (17) or alcohol (15), and more men (12 in 100) than women (about 6 in 100) who had used cannabis had been dependent. The 2001 to 2005 survey estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime and about 6 in 100 within 10 years of first use; for half of the people who became dependent, it began within about 5 years. Today's diagnosis, cannabis use disorder, also counts milder cases, and newer US figures, such as 3 in 10 among people who used in the past year, count only people using recently. Both surveys are from the US, from 1990 to 2005, before today's stronger products.
set.magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE: dependence assessed in a subsample of 4,414, use taken from the 1991 NHSDA); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; half of the cases of dependence about 5 years after first use (a median among people who became dependent). Second-hand: about 1 in 10 of people who use regularly (Connor et al., 2021, citing a UN report; Hall, 2015, abstract); about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015); 3 in 10 people who used in the past year meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis).
set.grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions in survey populations): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: two independent national probability surveys, a decade apart and with different instruments and DSM versions, give about 9 in 100, and the claim states their measures, years and populations. Strict reading: the 2001-05 timing figures (5.9% within 10 years, about 2% in the first year, half of the cases within about 5 years) rest on recalled ages and an actuarial curve without intervals and on their own would be rated down one level for risk of bias, to very low. The narrative reviews and the 2020 professional statement are used only to trace the figure they repeat, to show the other denominators behind higher figures, and for the DSM-5 definition; they add no data, and the 30% and 3 in 10 they cite for newer data are second-hand and on other denominators and do not enter the rating. Overlap: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and Connor et al. (2021) take their 9% from the 1990-92 survey or a chapter by its first author (Connor's other 1 in 10 figures come from a UN report), and Volkow et al. (2014) and Curran et al. (2016) from the 2001-05 analysis, so the reviews are not further replication. Status replicated: the two surveys are independent and agree.

set.statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by Connor et al., 2021); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015; its title refers to frequent use); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced, and repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020). No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter for both figures; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt for one in six, with 17% in its table, and the 2001-05 survey analysis for 9%); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used, and note that differences between age groups may also reflect birth cohort, period and drug availability, and that deaths linked to dependence remove dependent people from older groups (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one in the adjusted model (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), a model that stepwise selection built from sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders, and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (mood disorders, 2.69, and cocaine dependence, 4.14, among others, went with higher hazards); the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the psychiatric and substance use disorders that go with it, and that people who start later may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). Because that model also adjusted for disorders that may have begun after first use, the reversal does not show that starting early protects against dependence (editors' reading). In a 3-year prospective study, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016, which calls its sample people who used daily; its title refers to frequent use), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: Reviews report that people who use cannabis more often are more likely to be dependent: figures for people who use daily run from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2, depending on the study, and one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study. Reviews also say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used. But in a large US survey, starting before age 14 went with more dependence only until other mental health and drug problems were taken into account; after that, it went with less. That does not mean starting early protects: some of those problems may have come after people started. So it is not clear whether starting young itself raises the risk or whether people who start young are at higher risk for other reasons. Most of these numbers are second-hand, and none of these studies can show cause. See the contested question.
set.magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable; repeated without a citation by Page 2020). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14 (1,051 people, unweighted) against 14 or later (6,339): unadjusted HR 2.47 (95% CI 2.0 to 3.1); adjusted 0.63 (0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model male sex 1.44, age 18-29 3.09 and 30-44 2.46 (against 45 or older), mood disorder 2.69, anxiety disorder 2.31, personality disorder 2.30, nicotine dependence 2.06, alcohol dependence 2.55, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6).
set.exposure: Frequency of use (weekly, daily, regular, a history of daily use, frequent use, as each source defined it) and age at first use (adolescence, before 16, before 14); in one survey, age at interview
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Surveys and cohorts with self-reported, often recalled, use and ages; the age figures are unadjusted except in NESARC, where adjustment reversed the direction but conditioned on mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates, some of which may follow early use; most frequency figures come with no adjustment set or definition (cards sc_anthony_1994, sc_lopez_quintero_2011, sc_connor_2021).
set.debate.evidence_yes: Every source that reports dependence by frequency finds more in people who use more often: 17.0% of people who smoked weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021); a UN report gives about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily, and two reviews 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (all as cited by Connor et al., 2021); and a 3-year prospective study is cited for half of people using daily (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015), against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (see the claim on how many people become dependent). For age of starting, reviews give one in six of people who start in adolescence (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Volkow et al., 2014), describe people who start in adolescence as 2 to 4 times as likely as adult starters to show dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014), and cite first use before 16 as raising the risk and speeding progression (Connor et al., 2021). In the 1990-92 US survey, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of 15- to 24-year-olds who had used cannabis had ever been dependent, against 8.1% to 8.5% at 25 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years at risk, and its authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). Reviews also name concurrent tobacco use and male sex as risk factors (Curran et al., 2016).
set.debate.evidence_no: In the one national analysis read that modelled age of first use together with other risk factors (NESARC, 2001-05; 7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence), first use before 14 went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (2.47) but a lower one in a model chosen by stepwise selection that kept sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the disorders that go with it, and that later starters may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). A 3-year prospective study found that measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016). Twin studies show genetic influence on starting early after allowing for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety, and shared genetic or environmental factors contribute to early onset (Connor et al., 2021); a review names poor school achievement, deviant behaviour, rebelliousness, poor relationships with parents and parents' drug and alcohol problems as marking higher risk (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). The widely quoted 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily is cited to a review that does not contain it (Volkow et al., 2014) and is repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020), and the age-group figures from the 1990-92 survey are by age at interview, not age at first use, and may also reflect birth cohort, period, availability and deaths in older groups (Anthony et al., 1994).
set.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). More frequent use goes with more dependence in every source that reports it, but the size depends on design and definition (from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 2 of people using daily), most figures are second-hand, and one widely quoted figure cannot be traced. For age of starting, the crude figures point to more dependence in early starters, but the one national analysis that adjusted for other disorders found the opposite, which fits early starting being a marker of other risks at least as well as a cause; because that analysis also adjusted for disorders that may follow early use, it does not show that early starting protects, and the evidence read here does not settle which reading is right.

set.statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, differed greatly by where the samples came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32); like the differences by setting, these are comparisons between groups of studies, not within the same people. The one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; counted by participants it is about 28 in 100 (the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518, is 27.5%, editors' calculation, and its forest plot's fixed-effect total, which gives larger cohorts more weight, is 0.28). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, as two reviews summarise it, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms developing within about a week after heavy and prolonged use stops (Bahji et al., 2020, which also word it as within 7 days of reduced use; Connor et al., 2021): irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and a physical symptom such as headache, sweating or stomach pain, with distress or impairment that Connor et al. describe as clinically severe. Many of these symptoms also occur in withdrawal from other substances and in other mental disorders (Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021), while a 2020 professional statement describes a longer course, beginning a few days after stopping or cutting down, peaking at about 10 days and ending after 30 days (Page et al., 2020); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent (Curran et al., 2016), and irritability, sleep difficulty, low mood, craving and anxiety are listed by Volkow et al. (2014); people seeking help to stop report symptoms that include anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), which a later review by the same first author calls the most common symptoms, often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016). On medical risk the sources disagree without evidence: one review says that, in people without other medical or psychiatric illness, withdrawal does not pose serious risks and usually needs only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021), while the 2020 professional statement advises clinicians to tell people who use heavily over the long term not to stop suddenly because of the risk of withdrawal (Page et al., 2020); neither cites a study for this. In one laboratory study, oral THC given by the researchers eased the symptoms (Budney et al., 2007, as cited by Curran et al., 2016), and in trials the THC medicines dronabinol and nabiximols reduced withdrawal symptoms but did not reduce cannabis use compared with a placebo (Curran et al., 2016). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: When people who use cannabis regularly stop or cut down, some get withdrawal: irritability or anger, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood, or physical symptoms such as headaches. A 2020 review found it in about 17 in 100 people with regular use in general-population surveys, 54 in 100 in outpatient groups and 87 in 100 in inpatient groups; withdrawal at any time in life was reported much more often than in the past year. Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks, though one professional statement says it can last about a month. Expert sources disagree on whether it carries any medical risk, and none gives evidence for its view. The studies defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways, many of the same feelings also come with other conditions, and none checked how often they occur in people who do not cut down.
set.magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22 in Table 2; 13 to 21 in the text; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357 in the text, 359 in Figure 2); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52 in the abstract, 27 to 37 in the Results text; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); Figure 2 totals: random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55), fixed effect 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Participant count: 6,469 of 23,518 in the abstract (27.5%, editors' calculation; cohort sizes times prevalences in Table 1 sum to 6,470). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks; in one professional statement, onset after a few days, peak at about 10 days, end after 30 days.
set.outcome: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome as each study defined and measured it (rating scales, checklists and diagnostic interviews; most cohorts used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for the use disorder), at any time in life or in the past year; symptoms and time course as described in reviews
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Regular use undefined; most definitions predate DSM-5; the pools include a prison survey and a synthetic-cannabinoid detoxification sample; the symptom description and time course are second-hand (narrative reviews and a professional statement), and these sources differ on the time course (1 to 2 weeks against about 30 days).
set.grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in the populations sampled): starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. The headline 47% is not used as the answer, because it averages cohorts of very different kinds and tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant (card sc_bahji_2020; the review's own fixed-effect total is 0.28); the setting-specific figures are. The narrative reviews describe symptoms and time course second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Connor et al., 2021, take their 54% and 87% from it, relabelled), so they are not counted as further studies. Status replicated: in 50 cohorts from many teams withdrawal was found in some people who used regularly, consistently more often in clinical samples; how often varies widely, which the inconsistency rating carries.

set.statement: In published cases of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, again and again, in people who use cannabis regularly), pooled descriptively in a systematic review of reports from 2000 to September 2015 (Sorensen et al., 2017; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 211 patients from 80 case reports and 7 case series, 98 of them from one series entered as summary figures; no randomized trials, no comparison groups and no count of how many people who use cannabis develop the syndrome), all patients had recurrent vomiting with severe nausea and 85.1% had abdominal pain; 154 of 211 (72.9%) were men; among the 113 patients with individual data, the median age was 16 at first cannabis use (IQR 14 to 18; 84 patients), 24 at the start of symptoms (19 to 29; 101) and 28 at diagnosis (22 to 34; 111). Of the 197 whose frequency of use was reported, 76.6% used cannabis daily or more often and 97.4% at least weekly (the reviewers counted reports of heavy use as daily and of frequent use as weekly), and 45 of 179 (25.1%) had used for a year or less before symptoms began. Of the patients whose bathing was reported, 157 of 170 (92.3%) found that hot baths or showers relieved their symptoms. Of the 64 patients whose stopping was documented, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine test to confirm that they had stopped, and all 21 patients who kept using still had symptoms. The review's tables differ on the details: its main table counts relief after abstinence or reduction and places one of the two patients without resolution in a case series rather than in the case reports the text cites, and another table describes a patient in the 98-patient series who did not improve despite reported abstinence, a patient the main table leaves out of the count. Follow-up was documented for only 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%), no time to resolution is reported although it was among the data to be collected, and whether symptoms returned when people started again was too inconsistently documented to count, although in one series all 3 patients who used cannabis again after a period without it became ill again. The review proposes recognising the syndrome by severe cyclic vomiting, usually with abdominal pain, at least weekly cannabis use before symptoms began, temporary relief with hot bathing and resolution after stopping, with male sex, starting cannabis in the teenage years and symptoms beginning in the twenties as supporting features; these features come from cases diagnosed by them, so their frequencies do not show how well they separate the syndrome from other causes of repeated vomiting, which no study in the review tested. In second-hand surveys of patients diagnosed with cyclic vomiting syndrome, 72% of 31 and 67% of 437 also used hot showers for relief, although many of them used cannabis (42% daily to weekly in the first; 81% in the second). Diagnosis came on average 4.1 years (SD 4.6) after symptoms began, and in four case reports patients first diagnosed with severe vomiting of pregnancy, whose cyclic vomiting had begun before the pregnancy, were later diagnosed with the syndrome. A 2021 review says the distinction from other cyclic vomiting disorders is underdeveloped and gives 90% of patients as reporting that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms, citing a 2019 clinical review and Sorensen et al. (2017) itself and merging two features that the systematic review counts separately (Connor et al., 2021; second-hand), and a 2014 review links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation (Volkow et al., 2014). All nine proposed mechanisms were rated very low, and three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids; acute hospital treatments are covered in the claims on capsaicin cream and on dopamine-blocking medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, usually with belly pain, in people who use cannabis regularly. In 211 published cases, about three in four used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before the bouts began, and most found that hot baths or showers eased the symptoms for a while, though many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too. Of the 64 cases where stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better, and the 21 people who kept using did not. These are published cases only: nobody knows from them how common the syndrome is, fewer than half of the cases had any follow-up written down, and the signs used to recognise it come from the same cases, so how well they tell it apart from other vomiting illnesses has not been tested. On average it took about 4 years from the first symptoms to the diagnosis.
set.magnitude: Sorensen 2017 cumulative synthesis (211 patients; each share is of the patients in whom the feature was reported): recurrent vomiting 100% (211); severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211); abdominal pain 85.1% (202); relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170); resolution after stopping 96.8% (62 of 64; all 21 who kept using had ongoing symptoms); at least weekly use 97.4% (197); daily or more 76.6% (197); regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179); men 72.9% (154 of 211). Duration of use before onset (179): 1 year or less 25.1%, 2-5 years 36.3%, 6-10 years 16.8%, 11 years or more 21.8%. Median ages, from the 113 patients with individual data: first use 16 (IQR 14-18; 84), onset 24 (19-29; 101), diagnosis 28 (22-34; 111). Mean delay to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6). Follow-up documented for 85 of 211 (40.2%). One series: all 3 patients who resumed after abstinence relapsed. Second-hand, cyclic vomiting syndrome surveys: hot showers used by 72% of 31 (42% using cannabis daily to weekly) and 67% of 437 (81% using cannabis).
set.grade.reasoning: Case reports and series are observational and start low; down two levels for risk of bias (selection, circular diagnosis, incomplete follow-up) and one for indirectness: very low, the floor. Status replicated: the same picture (recurrent vomiting with regular use, relief with hot water, resolution after stopping) comes from many case reports and several series by different teams, though they reach the claim through one review and the series inside it are not counted again (card sc_sorensen_2017). Connor et al. (2021) take their 90% from a 2019 clinical review and from Sorensen et al. (2017) itself, so it is not separate evidence. The resolution figure describes documented cases, not what happens to everyone who stops, and the review's own tables differ on its details.

set.statement: As summarised in a 2007 narrative review of controlled-administration studies, most of them small, often with single doses of low-THC cigarettes or of oral THC given by researchers, many from the author's own laboratory and with participants' sex given for only a few of them (Huestis, 2007; figures second-hand; no systematic search), smoked THC, compared with THC taken by mouth, is associated with THC reaching the blood within minutes rather than hours, with higher and earlier peaks, and after frequent or heavy use THC and its breakdown products remained detectable for days to weeks. Smoked: in 6 people (the review does not give their sex) who smoked single cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg; study conditions), THC appeared in plasma with the first puff, peaked at a mean of 84.3 and 162.2 ng/ml at 9.0 minutes, fell to about 60% and 20% of the peak 15 and 30 minutes after smoking, and was 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours, staying detectable (at 0.5 ng/ml) for 3 to 12 hours after the lower and 6 to 27 hours after the higher dose; the strongest effects came later, 30 to 45 minutes after smoking began, when blood levels were already falling. How much of the THC in a cigarette reached the blood varied with how people smoked, from 2% to 56% across studies (about 8% to 24% in others, depending strongly on experience with smoking cannabis). By mouth: THC was absorbed more slowly, with lower, later and more irregular peaks; after 20 mg of THC in a chocolate cookie, plasma peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml came 1 to 5 hours after eating, with about 6% of the dose reaching the blood, and a study using a radiolabel method, which the author says overestimated THC, found peaks about 4 to 6 hours after 15 to 20 mg in oil; the review puts oral bioavailability at 4% to 20%, because THC is partly broken down in the stomach and much of it is converted in the liver, among other products into 11-OH-THC, which is active and reaches levels similar to or higher than those of THC after oral intake, against about a tenth of THC after smoking. In the studies described, effects after oral THC began later and lasted longer than after smoking. THC is almost entirely bound to lipoproteins in the blood (95% to 99%) and is stored in body fat; in people who use frequently, its final plasma half-life was about 4.1 days in a study with long sampling (24 to 36 hours in studies with shorter sampling), which the review attributes to storage in and slow release from fat, and THC-COOH, the breakdown product that urine tests measure, had a plasma half-life of up to 12.6 days in one person; the review notes that no pharmacokinetic differences between frequent and occasional use have been substantiated. Plasma: in people who use frequently, low levels remained at least 12 hours after last use (THC 0.86 ng/ml on average in one study; whole-blood levels are about half those in plasma), and after people who used chronically smoked four cigarettes containing labelled THC, a very sensitive method detected it in blood for up to 13 days. Urine: after one smoked cigarette (6 people), the last positive sample for THC-COOH at a cut-off of 15 ng/ml came an average of 33.7 hours (8 to 68.5) after the 1.75% and 88.6 hours (57 to 122.3) after the 3.55% cigarette, with positive and negative samples alternating near the cut-off, while the urine of a person new to cannabis may test negative within a few hours of one cigarette; one person who had used heavily for more than 10 years still tested positive (above 20 ng/ml) 67 days after last use, a case the review calls extreme, and in another person with heavy use cannabinoids were detectable in urine for 93 days (no cut-off given). A positive urine test shows that a person was exposed, not when, how much, by which route or whether they were impaired. These studies predate today's stronger products, edibles, vaporizers and concentrates, gave fixed doses and, where the review gives participants' sex, mostly involved men, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In small lab studies from before 2007, in which people smoked weak cannabis cigarettes, THC in the blood was highest within minutes of smoking (at about 9 minutes) and fell to low levels within 2 hours, while the felt effects were strongest a little later, at 30 to 45 minutes. When THC was taken by mouth, it entered the blood slowly and at lower levels, peaking 1 to 6 hours later, and the effects began later and lasted longer. THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it could still be found for days to weeks. After one cigarette, the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and the urine of someone new to cannabis may test negative within hours; in one person who had used heavily for years, urine was still positive after 67 days, and in another, cannabis could be found for 93 days. A positive test shows use, not when, how much or whether someone was impaired. The studies gave set doses, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more.
set.magnitude: Smoked (6 people; sex not given in the review): mean plasma THC peaks 84.3 ng/ml (range 50-129) and 162.2 ng/ml (76-267) at 9.0 minutes; about 60% and 20% of peak at 15 and 30 minutes; 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours; detectable at 0.5 ng/ml for 3-12 and 6-27 hours; peak effects 30-45 minutes after smoking began; bioavailability 2%-56% (or about 8%-24%). Oral: 20 mg in a cookie, peaks 4.4-11 ng/ml at 1-5 hours, bioavailability about 6%; 15-20 mg in oil, peaks at about 4-6 hours (radiolabel); 10 mg dronabinol (17 volunteers), THC 3.8 ng/ml (1.1-12.7), 11-OH-THC 3.4 (1.2-5.6), THC-COOH 26 (14-46) at 1-2 hours; summary bioavailability 4%-20%; 11-OH-THC about 10% of THC after smoking, similar or higher after oral intake. Elimination: terminal plasma THC half-life about 4.1 days with frequent use (24-36 hours with shorter sampling); THC-COOH plasma half-life up to 12.6 days in one person; no pharmacokinetic difference between frequent and occasional use substantiated; frequent use, plasma THC 0.86 ng/ml at least 12 hours after last use; deuterated THC detectable in blood up to 13 days after four labelled cigarettes (limit 0.02 ng/ml). Urine (6 people, 15 ng/ml cut-off): last positive 33.7 hours (8-68.5) and 88.6 hours (57-122.3) after one cigarette; a person new to cannabis may test negative within a few hours; heavy use, positive up to 67 days (20 ng/ml; one case, called extreme) and cannabinoids detectable for 93 days (no cut-off given) in two individuals.
set.population: People given cannabis or THC in small controlled-administration studies summarised by a 2007 narrative review (6 people, sex not given, in the main smoking and urine studies; 17 volunteers in a capsule study; where the review gives participants' sex, mostly men), and single case reports of heavy long-term use
set.exposure: Single smoked cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg) or oral THC (20 mg in a cookie; 15 to 20 mg in oil; a 10 mg dronabinol capsule), given by researchers (study conditions only); frequent or heavy long-term use for elimination and detection windows
set.comparator: Smoking compared with taking THC by mouth; frequent compared with occasional use
